evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Fraxinus pennsylvanica and lists Texas within its native range.
Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list includes F. pennsylvanica; UT PRC documents naturally occurring green ash in north Hays County.
USDA PLANTS-derived county native-status data records F. pennsylvanica as native in Bell County.
The same USDA-derived county data records it as native in Comal County.
target_zone_range.guardrail: The Central Texas F. albicans/F. pennsylvanica boundary can be messy and UT PRC notes possible hybridization; fruit plus leaf scar plus lower-leaf surface should outweigh leaf silhouette alone.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at the samara first: green ash has a larger seed body with the wing decurrent well down the body before abruptly broadening; then confirm a broad shield-shaped leaf scar and usually non-glaucous lower leaflet surface.
diagnostic_traits: opposite branches and odd-pinnate leaves, usually 5–7(–9) leaflets
leaflet margins subentire to inconspicuously dentate-serrulate
abaxial leaflet surface generally glabrous rather than densely white-waxy
leaf scar shield-shaped to broadly oblong-ovate, upper edge truncate to only shallowly concave
samara consistently 2-winged in the Central Texas key
samara body >1.5 cm; wing runs down the proximal portion of the body then broadens distally

confusers.separator: Priority comparison. Texas ash has a glaucous/waxy lower leaflet surface, smaller fruit body, and wing only slightly decurrent; green ash has a larger body and more strongly decurrent wing.
Mexican ash tends toward 3–5 leaflets, coarse sharp distal serration, smaller shallower leaf scars, and occasional 3-winged fruits.
White ash typically has more strongly stalked leaflets and a deeply U-notched leaf scar embracing the bud.
